cues.text: Start with the dicot root section.
A marks the outer epiblema, also called the root epidermis.
B points into the broad cortex.
C ends on the endodermis, the innermost cortical layer, and D identifies the
pericycle just inside it.
These concentric outlines locate tissue boundaries; their thickness does not
measure the number of cells.
Root hairs, passage cells and Casparian strips are not individually drawn.
In a typical young root, lateral roots originate from the pericycle, not by
extending a root hair.
Trace each leader to its endpoint before naming the layer.
The central vascular region is distinct from the surrounding cortex.
Focus on the central four armed region labelled X.
It represents xylem, with the P marked phloem groups between the arms.
Xylem and phloem occupy alternating radial positions, so this is a radial
arrangement rather than a collateral stem bundle.
The diagram illustrates a tetrarch example, not the only possible dicot root
pattern.
Primary root xylem is exarch: protoxylem occurs toward the periphery and
metaxylem toward the centre.
This describes the developmental position of xylem, not a horizontal arrow of
water movement through the root.
Do not infer a prominent central pith from the empty background of this
selected structure sketch.
Now use the monocot root section.
A is the conspicuous central pith.
Around it, eight X marked xylem groups alternate with P marked phloem groups.
More than six xylem poles illustrates the polyarch condition commonly
emphasised for monocot roots.
The groups surround the pith, but xylem and phloem remain on alternate radii:
do not call them collateral bundles just because they lie around a circle.
The cortex and enclosing boundaries are simplified, and the exact count drawn
is not a species diagnosis.
Compare both root figures using several features together: the pith, the
number
of poles and the radial tissue arrangement.
Compare the two roots without reducing the task to one memorised outline.
Both show radial vascular organisation and the exarch primary xylem pattern.
The monocot example has many poles and a prominent pith, while the dicot
example has four xylem arms and no prominent pith represented.
Typical monocot roots do not undergo the conventional vascular cambium
secondary growth familiar from many dicots.
That comparison does not mean every dicot root already has a visible cambium
ring in an early primary section.
Developmental stage matters.
A single simplified section supports a structural interpretation, not an
absolute identification of every species or its age.
Move to the two stem sections.
A illustrates a young dicot stem with vascular bundles arranged in a ring
around the central pith.
B illustrates a typical monocot stem with bundles scattered through the ground
tissue.
Each small symbol represents an entire bundle rather than a single cell.
Bundle size and spacing have been simplified, so do not count the symbols to
name a species.
Unlike the root panels, these stem bundles contain xylem and phloem together
on
the same radius.
The stem comparison concerns primary anatomy; a mature woody stem can look
very
different after secondary growth.
Establish organ and developmental context before applying a visual rule.
Use the symbol key beneath the stem sections.
The short bar represents phloem toward the outside of each bundle, and the
circle represents xylem toward the centre of the stem.
In a typical collateral stem bundle, both tissues lie along the same radius.
Primary stem xylem is endarch: protoxylem is closer to the centre, with
metaxylem farther outward.
The small circles here stand for xylem regions and do not separately resolve
those developmental stages.
Do not use inward and outward tissue positions as arrows for sugar movement.
Phloem transport follows source and sink relationships rather than being
permanently downward in every sieve tube.
The enlarged bundle board labels A as open and B as closed.
Read outside at the top and centre at the bottom.
In A, phloem lies above the thick line representing vascular cambium, and
xylem
lies below it.
B has phloem and xylem but no intervening vascular cambium.
Open therefore refers to cambium and its capacity to add vascular tissues, not
to a hole for water.
Typical dicot stem bundles are open collateral bundles, while typical monocot
stem bundles are closed collateral bundles.
The absence of a line in a poor micrograph alone would not prove absence of
cambium; this labelled schematic explicitly states what is represented.
Finish with the selected cell sketches.
C represents a vessel element, with wall pits and a perforated end that
connects with other elements in a vessel.
A functional mature vessel element lacks a living protoplast.
D shows a sieve tube element beside a companion cell.
The marked end is a sieve plate, and the nucleus drawn beside the tube belongs
to the companion cell.
A mature angiosperm sieve tube element is living but lacks its own nucleus.
Do not conclude that all xylem cells are dead: xylem parenchyma is living.
Similarly, phloem includes more than sieve tubes and companion cells,
including
typically dead fibres.
These are selected components of complex tissues, not complete tissue
inventories.
